title: bundled: fix build against Linux kernels older than 5.1
body:
Buildroot 2026.05.x fails when targeting linux kernels < 5.1 due to compilation error in `strace` version 7.0. Buildroot HEAD works around this by [disabling strace builds on older kernels.](https://github.com/buildroot/buildroot/blob/master/package/strace/Config.in) Alternatively, we can apply the same backwards-compatibility mechanism used elsewhere in  `strace` and maintain support for older kernels. 

---
Header <linux/time_types.h> was introduced in kernel 5.1 with commit ca5e9aba753e ("time: Add time_types.h").

Apply the same backward-compatibility shim used in io_uring.h allowing callers to replace <linux/time_types.h> with kernel_time_types.h.

* bundled/linux/include/uapi/linux/taskstats.h: Guard with UAPI_LINUX_TASKSTATS_H_SKIP_LINUX_TIME_TYPES_H.
* src/netlink_nlctrl.c: Include kernel_time_types.h and define UAPI_LINUX_TASKSTATS_H_SKIP_LINUX_TIME_TYPES_H.
* tests/netlink_nlctrl.c: Likewise.

title: make output terminal width aware and indent overflown lines
body: `strace` has options to make it's output more verbose which can be incredibly useful for debugging and clarity, however, this often makes lots of syscalls output lines which are longer than the terminal width. the current behaviour is that strace simply does not tackle this and the lines are overflown by the terminal. This makes it hard to parse the output visually, as the syscall invocations are interleaved with the overflown lines. I wish that strace queried the width of the terminal, and broke the new lines and indented them itself, to make the output easier to parse. Something like this: This may be undesirable for greppability and non-terminal output, so it would be gated behind a CLI flag. I'd be down to give implementing this a shot, if you think this makes sense.

title: setns: decode namespace transition with --namespace=new option even if nstype is 0
body:
When setns is called with nstype specified as 0, any type of namespace
can be joined and the type is determined by the passed fd. Query the
namespace type of the fd by reading the /proc/$pid/fd/$fd symlink to
retrieve the type of namespace being joined.

* NEWS: Mention this change.
* src/clone.c (read_namespace_type_for_fd): New helper function.
(get_namespace_auxstr): Add expected_ns_str parameter.
If flags is 0, print the namespace ID of expected_ns_str.
(SYS_FUNC(clone), SYS_FUNC(clone3), SYS_FUNC(unshare)): Pass NULL
as expected_ns_str to get_namespace_auxstr.
(SYS_FUNC(setns)): Query the namespace type of the joined fd
using read_namespace_type_for_fd if nstype is 0, and pass it as
expected_ns_str to get_namespace_auxstr.
* tests/setns-report-ns-id.c (main): Add a test case for setns(fd, 0).

title: strace -c segfaults in __strlen_avx2 during summary printing (heap-layout-dependent)
body:
## Environment

- strace 6.8
- Linux 6.17.0-35-generic x86_64
- Ubuntu 24.04.1
- glibc 2.39, GCC 13.3.0

## Description

`strace -c` segfaults during summary printing with certain syscall patterns. The traced program completes successfully (body written, exit 0), but strace itself crashes with SIGSEGV in `__strlen_avx2` when generating the summary after the child exits.

## Reproduction

```sh
git clone https://github.com/anomalyco/curldbg.git
cd curldbg
make
python3 tests/server.py &
strace -c ./curldbg -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:9999/get
```

Expected: summary table printed, exit 0. Actual: segfault, exit 139.

The crash is **not in the traced program**:
- `strace` without `-c` works fine (shows `+++ exited with 0 +++`)
- `strace -C` works fine
- The body is written correctly before strace segfaults

## Heap-layout dependent

The same binary with identical flags to an HTTPS target works fine, confirming the crash depends on memory layout:

```
# Works (exit 0, 233 syscalls):
strace -c ./curldbg -s -o /dev/null https://httpbin.org/get

# Crashes (exit 139, ~200 syscalls):
strace -c ./curldbg -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:9999/get
```

The TLS code path loads libssl/libcrypto which shifts heap layout and avoids the corruption. Without TLS, the bug manifests 100% of the time.

## Backtrace

```
(gdb) bt
#0  __strlen_avx2 () at ../sysdeps/x86_64/multiarch/strlen-avx2.S:76
#1  0x00005555555e5f66 in strace summary-printing code
#2  0x00007ffff7c2a1ca in __libc_start_call_main
```

## Additional notes

- `strace -c -e trace=close ./curldbg ...` also crashes (only tracing close + exit_group is enough)
- The crash occurs during `exit_group` processing when strace formats its internal summary table
- It appears to be a NULL or corrupted string pointer being passed to `strlen()` by strace's own data structures

## Workaround

Use `strace -C` instead of `strace -c` for collecting the summary.

title: Bundled headers update did not add time_types.h
body:
Linux fixed  timespec64 definition in _90079798f1d7 ("delayacct: fix uapi timespec64 definition")_ and since then `linux/taskstats.h` needs `linux/time_types.h`. This change was brought into strace with 33b9507, which didn't add `linux/time_types.h` so the build fails with:
```
In file included from ../bundled/linux/include/uapi/linux/cgroupstats.h:20,
                 from netlink_nlctrl.c:11:
../bundled/linux/include/uapi/linux/taskstats.h:21:10: fatal error: linux/time_types.h: No such file or directory
   21 | #include <linux/time_types.h>
      |          ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

Sorry for not providing PR right away; `linux/time_types.h` needs `__kernel_old_time_t`:
```
In file included from ../bundled/linux/include/uapi/linux/taskstats.h:21,
                 from ../bundled/linux/include/uapi/linux/cgroupstats.h:20,
                 from netlink_nlctrl.c:11:
../bundled/linux/include/uapi/linux/time_types.h:32:9: error: unknown type name '__kernel_old_time_t'; did you mean '__kernel_old_gid_t'?
   32 |         __kernel_old_time_t     tv_sec;         /* seconds */
      |         ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
      |         __kernel_old_gid_t
```
That's in `asm/posix_types.h` included through `linux/types.h`, but despite later is in tree for a long time, the former is not, thus I wonder how is `--enable-bundled` supposed to work.

title: Give a hint about yama if strace -p fails on EPERM
body:
If strace -p fails on EPERM and the PID matches, the reason is not clean. Give a hint that yama could block it.

It displays the extended message if the error is EPERM and UID is not 0. There are some "false matches" as advanced checks like UID match would require parsing of /proc/$PID/status.

title: Error when compiling with Android NDK: unknown type name 'in_addr_t'
body:
Both the latest LTS (r27d) and latest stable (r29) NDK versions produce the same error.

Steps to reproduce:
```
git clone https://github.com/strace/strace.git
cd strace
./bootstrap

NDK_PATH=/path/to/ndk
TOOLCHAIN="${NDK_PATH}/toolchains/llvm/prebuilt/linux-x86_64"
export CC="${TOOLCHAIN}/bin/aarch64-linux-android35-clang"
export AR="${TOOLCHAIN}/bin/llvm-ar"
export RANLIB="${TOOLCHAIN}/bin/llvm-ranlib"
export STRIP="${TOOLCHAIN}/bin/llvm-strip"
./configure --host=aarch64-linux-android35 --target=aarch64-linux-android35 --disable-mpers --disable-gcc-Werror
make
```

The build will fail with the following error:
```
/path/to/ndk/toolchains/llvm/prebuilt/linux-x86_64/bin/../sysroot/usr/include/arpa/inet.h:40:1: error: unknown type name 'in_addr_t'
   40 | in_addr_t inet_addr(const char* _Nonnull __s);
      | ^
```

A workaround I found is to set `export CFLAGS="-Din_addr_t=uint32_t"`.

title: count: add wall-* column aliases for -c summary report
body:
Closes #327.

Adds wall-clock-aware column aliases (`wall-total`, `wall-min`, `wall-max`, `wall-avg`) to the `-c` summary report. These always read wall-clock data regardless of `-w`, so wall and CPU times can be rendered side by side via `-U` in a single `strace` run instead of two.

Existing column aliases keep their current polymorphic semantics with respect to `-w` (backward compatible).

### Before — two runs required

```
$ strace -c sh -c 'sleep 0.05; head -c 32K /dev/urandom > /dev/null'
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ----------------
 57.70    0.002521         630         4         2 wait4
 21.01    0.000918          13        68        64 newfstatat
  3.94    0.000172          86         2           vfork
...

$ strace -cw sh -c 'sleep 0.05; head -c 32K /dev/urandom > /dev/null'
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ----------------
 92.39    0.054119       13529         4         2 wait4
  2.72    0.001591          23        68        64 newfstatat
  1.60    0.000937         468         2           vfork
...
```

Numbers drift between runs because timing is non-deterministic.

### After — one run, both timings

```
$ strace -c -U time-total,wall-total,calls,errors,name -S wall-total \
      sh -c 'sleep 0.05; head -c 32K /dev/urandom > /dev/null'
    seconds  wall-total     calls    errors syscall
----------- ----------- --------- --------- ----------------
   0.003380    0.053591         4         2 wait4
   0.000446    0.001481        68        64 newfstatat
   0.000131    0.000752         2           vfork
   0.000000    0.000289         1           execve
...
```

Same workload, both timings captured. `wait4` ratio (~16× wall/CPU) is now visible directly.

### Tests

`tests/count.test` extended with five new pattern checks covering `-U time-total,wall-total,...`, `-U wall-{total,min,max},...`, and `-S wall-total`. Local run: `count.test` and `count-f.test` PASS.

body:
## Summary

Fixes #380 — glibc 2.43 declares `bsearch()` as returning `const void *` under C23 mode, causing a "discards const qualifier" error when assigning to `const struct_ioctlent *` without an explicit cast.

## Changes

`src/ioctl.c`: Add explicit `(const struct_ioctlent *)` cast on the `bsearch()` return value in `ioctl_lookup()`.

## Error (before fix)

```
src/ioctl.c: In function 'ioctl_lookup':
src/ioctl.c:52:13: error: assignment discards 'const' qualifier from pointer target type [-Werror=discarded-qualifiers]
   52 | iop = bsearch((const void *) (const uintptr_t) code, ioctlent,
      | ^
```

## Notes

- The same `bsearch()` call in `src/xlat.c` (line 89) does not need a fix — its target variable is already `const struct xlat_data *` and the const-qualified return from glibc 2.43's `bsearch()` is compatible without a cast.
- Also removed the unnecessary `const` from `(const uintptr_t)` — `uintptr_t` is not const-qualified so the cast is misleading.

title: Add support for tracking unknown syscalls in summary mode
body:
Related to issue #319 

This patch introduces support for unknown syscalls tracking in summary mode (-c/-C).
It prepares the codebase for integrating unknown syscall accounting into statistics output.

Previously, syscalls with unknown numbers were ignored in summary mode, resulting in incomplete statistics.
This change adds a separate dynamic bucket for unknown syscalls and the necessary tracking logic.
No changes to output formatting or final statistics aggregation are included yet.

Changes:
- Add unknown syscall tracking infrastructure (src/count.c)
- Introduce unknown syscall storage (src/unknown_count.c)
- Add public declarations (src/count.h)

title: v4l2: decode `VIDIOC_QUERYMENU`
body:
Decode the `VIDIOC_QUERYMENU` ioctl, which is used for both string and integer menu controls. Unfortunately without querying the type of the control it is not possible to know if it is a string or integer, so print both.

Integer menus:

  ioctl(3, VIDIOC_QUERYMENU, {id=V4L2_CTRL_CLASS_USER+0xf907, index=2} => {name="\2", value=2}) = 0 <0.000025>

String menus:

  ioctl(3, VIDIOC_QUERYMENU, {id=V4L2_CTRL_CLASS_USER+0xf904, index=1} => {name="Menu Item 1", value=7310548498887107917}) = 0 <0.000039>

* src/v4l2.c: Decode `VIDIOC_QUERYMENU`.
* tests/ioctl_v4l2.c: Remove `VIDIOC_QUERYMENU` from the list of unsupported ioctls, and add some `VIDIOC_EXPBUF` tests.

body: I was amazed when `gdb` finally supported colors. but my favorite debugging tool `strace` was still plain output only. so i did something i've wanted for years: this is **colors for strace**! - in case you're using strace in an highest-performance environment, compile-time disable colors with `./configure --enable-colors=no` - there's a single branch checking if coloring is enabled in `color_seq` - i've set the default to `strace --color=auto`, which only enables colors if the output file (usually stderr) is a tty - i've used colors similar to the vim color scheme in `ft=strace`, so vim users don't have to adjust their eyes much - you can customize the color scheme using `STRACE_COLORS="syscall=91:constant=92" strace ls` (like `LS_COLORS`) - it detects your terminal background color luminance to select the bright/dark color theme defaults i'm very happy if you have any feedback! we'd like to include coloring in Ubuntu 26.04, so it would be great if you could quickly raise any concerns about coloring/this approach in general (since its feature freeze is very very soon). example output with `strace ls` in its source dir: closes #39

title: tests: Skip legacy_syscall_info on riscv64 with kernel 6.6.49+ too
body:
Follow-up to #330. See #315 for background.

---

Back in late 2024, strace commit ba41bc0da4b841d9 made it so that this test is skipped when running on kernel 6.11+, which is the first release containing kernel commit [61119394631f219e](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=61119394631f219e23ce98bcc3eb993a64a8ea64) ("riscv: entry: always initialize regs->a0 to -ENOSYS"), the one that broke the legacy API on riscv64.

What I failed to realize at the time is that the change had also been backported to the 6.6 tree as kernel commit [84557cd61182edf7](https://github.com/gregkh/linux/commit/84557cd61182edf7c776bd7d3284df5cacb22f7e), part of 6.6.49 stable kernel release. So we need to update our check to take that into account too, otherwise machines running an up-to-date LTS kernel will be unable to successfully build strace.

This theoretically makes us lose coverage for the 6.7 - 6.10 kernel range, but in reality 99% of riscv64 machines are running either the latest upstream kernel or a vendor kernel based on 6.6, so nothing really changes in practice.

title: Add standalone asinfo utility to map syscall names↔numbers and list syscalls
body:
A standalone utility that:
- Does not link against `libstrace` (avoids UI/runtime dependencies)
- Uses a generated header `asinfo_syscalls.h` built from `src/linux/<arch>/syscallent.h`
- Provides three modes:
  - `--to-names NR...`: Convert syscall numbers to names
  - `--to-numbers NAME...`: Convert syscall names to numbers  
  - `--list`: List all syscalls (format: `NUMBER NAME`)

### Build Integration

- **`src/Makefile.am`**:
  - Adds `asinfo` to `bin_PROGRAMS`
  - Generates `asinfo_syscalls.h` from `syscallent.h` at build time
  - Links `asinfo` standalone (no `libstrace` dependency)
  - Adds build rule dependencies

- **`Makefile.am`**:
  - Adds `doc/asinfo.1` to `man_MANS` for installation

### Documentation

- **`doc/asinfo.1`**: Manual page describing usage, options, and exit codes

### Testing

Four new test cases in `tests/`:
- **`asinfo.test`**: Basic roundtrip test (name → number → name)
- **`asinfo-multi.test`**: Multiple argument handling
- **`asinfo-errors.test`**: Error case validation (unknown names/numbers)
- **`asinfo-list.test`**: Verification that `--list` includes expected syscalls

All tests pass successfully.

### Packaging

- **`debian/strace.install`**: Installs `build/src/asinfo` to `/usr/bin`
- **`debian/strace.manpages`**: Installs `build/doc/asinfo.1` to man pages

## Usage Examples

```bash
# List all syscalls
$ asinfo --list | head -5
0 read
1 write
2 open
3 close
4 stat

# Convert name to number
$ asinfo --to-numbers read
0

# Convert number to name
$ asinfo --to-names 0
read

# Multiple conversions
$ asinfo --to-numbers read write open
0
1
2

$ asinfo --to-names 0 1 2
read
write
open
```

## Technical Details

### Syscall Table Generation

The `asinfo_syscalls.h` header is auto-generated at build time by parsing `src/linux/<arch>/syscallent.h`:

```c
static const char *asinfo_syscall_names[] = {
    [0] = "read",
    [1] = "write",
    // ... etc
};
static const unsigned int asinfo_syscall_count = ...;
```

title: kvm:  decode before and after states
body:
@ldv-alt I'm very sorry to make a pull request just after you merged #345.

However, I found a limitation in #345 that we cannot ignore.

I have tried the merged version of strace with the tracee available at https://github.com/masatake/kernel-essential-training/blob/master/kvm/add-iomem-kvm.c.
add-iomem-kvm.c demonstrates device emulation via I/O memory.

The tracee reads data from the address that has no memory-mapping.
In such a case, the tracee gains control with KVM_EXIT_IOMEM.
The tracee provides data via `run->mmio.data[0] = ` here `run` points memory region where kvm_run is mapped. Then the tracee invokes ioctl(KVM_RUN) to enter the guest mode.

I proposed `VCPU> ` in #345; strace mainly decoded the after-state of the kvm_run structure.
Though I considered decoding the difference between the before-state and after-state using tprint_value_changed, I found that my code was insufficient. I assumed exit_reason didn't change between the before-state and the after-state. e.g., When the guest exits with KVM_EXIT_IO, strace cannot decode the value of run->mmio.data[0] because the handler for KVM_EXIT_IOMEM decodes run->mmio.data[0].

In this pull request, I propose `VCPU< ` for decoding before-state and `VCPU> ` for decoding after-state.

```console
ioctl(5, KVM_RUN, 0)                    = 0 (KVM_EXIT_IO)
 VCPU:0< {..., exit_reason=6 /* KVM_EXIT_MMIO */, ..., {mmio={..., data=[0x3, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], len=1, is_write=0}}}
 VCPU:0> {..., exit_reason=2 /* KVM_EXIT_IO */, ..., {io={...}}}
```

Thank you for reading.

title: Testsuite fails with recent glibc if no vDSO
body:
Hi,

When running the testsuite on systems where there is no vDSO, the glibc malloc implementation might issue some `clock_gettime64`. It used to be fairly rare, but a [recent glibc patch](https://sourceware.org/git/?p=glibc.git;a=commit;h=a96a82c4a5efd3139e75cd11fd2a5554164dd5a0) made this much more likely. As a result we've started seeing [testsuite failures](https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/glibc/+bug/2125424) on Ubuntu armhf builders.

I wrote a [workaround](https://git.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/strace/tree/debian/patches/0004-Erase-clock_gettime64-calls-on-armhf.patch?h=import/6.16%2bds-2ubuntu2) to unblock the Ubuntu side, and I still don't know if the absence of vDSO is deliberate or not. If so, though, it's not a great long term solution, and in any case I figure I'd get the word out in case somebody else has similar issues.

title: Build failure in strace due to redefinition of struct sched_attr with glibc 2.41

Building strace fails when using glibc version 2.41. The error is caused by a conflicting definition of `struct sched_attr` between strace's bundled Linux headers and the system's glibc headers.

### Error snippet:
```
In file included from sched.c:14:
../bundled/linux/include/uapi/linux/sched/types.h:98:8: error: redefinition of 'struct sched_attr'
   98 | struct sched_attr {
      |        ^~~~~~~~~~
In file included from /x86_64-cross-linux-gnu/sys-root/include/sched.h:43,
                 from sched.c:13:
/x86_64-cross-linux-gnu/sys-root/lib64/gcc/x86_64-cross-linux-gnu/11.5.0/include-fixed/bits/sched.h:80:8: note: originally defined here
   80 | struct sched_attr
      |        ^~~~~~~~~~
```

### Root cause:
The `struct sched_attr` is now defined in glibc 2.41's headers, but strace also includes its own bundled Linux kernel headers which define the same struct, leading to a redefinition error.

glibc version: 2.41
Compiler: gcc 11.5.0
System: Linux x86_64

title: Symbols larger than 40 characters not printed with libunwind >= 1.8.0
body:
## Setup

This bug can be reproduced on x86_64 Linux with various strace versions >= 6.6

## Description

When configuring `--with-libunwind` (versions >= 1.8.0), and running with `-k`, the execution stack trace will not include function names for which the symbols have size larger than 40 characters, which is a [hardcoded limit when walking the stack](https://github.com/strace/strace/blob/ba20408d99c391c937453807285394117f8f3da7/src/unwind-libunwind.c#L119).

In my understanding, the expectation seems to be: in case this size isn't enough to fill a buffer with the found name, that `unw_get_proc_name()` would return `-UNW_ENOMEM`, and the [buffer would be adjusted](https://github.com/strace/strace/blob/ba20408d99c391c937453807285394117f8f3da7/src/unwind-libunwind.c#L61). However, due to what seems like a [libunwind bug](https://github.com/libunwind/libunwind/issues/922), this error code is no longer returned, and instead, we always get a single error `-UNW_ENOINFO`.

I'm also reporting this issue here for awareness, and in case it makes sense to implement some best effort workaround for these cases:

* Check if the buffer was filled after the call to `unw_get_proc_name()`, even if `-UNW_ENOINFO` is returned, and either print the (truncated) buffer contents, or fall-through to `xgrowarray()`;
* Allow `symbol_name_size` to be configurable (similar to what was done for `--stack-trace-frame-limit`), as any size that is large enough to cover the largest symbol name present will avoid this issue altogether, since `unw_get_proc_name()` will always successfully fill the provided buffer.

## Example (x86_64)

a.c:
```c
void a123456789_123456789_123456789_123456789() {
    asm("movl $0x3c,%eax\nsyscall\n");
}
void _start() {
    a123456789_123456789_123456789_123456789();
}
```

Observed output (affected frame has no symbol name, and offset is `+0x0`):
```
gcc -O0 -nostdlib -static a.c && strace -k ./a.out

execve("./a.out", ["./a.out"], 0x7ffc6a012908 /* 145 vars */) = 0
 > /tmp/a.out(_start+0x0) [0x100e]
exit(0)                                 = ?
+++ exited with 0 +++
 > /tmp/a.out(+0x0) [0x100b]
 > /tmp/a.out(_start+0xe) [0x101c]
 > unexpected_backtracing_error [0x1]
```

Expected output (frame with large symbol name and correct offset):
```
 > /tmp/a.out(a123456789_123456789_123456789_123456789+0xb) [0x100b]
```

title: Some tests are sensitive to load
body:
We (yoctoproject.org) run the strace test suite and have noticed that a number of tests are sensitive to system load and occasionally fail.

We're currently skipping clock_nanosleep, delay, nanosleep, and strace-r.

From experience I group load-sensitive tests into three categories:
1) Genuinely sensitive to load because the test has timeouts that need to be low, so the test _must_ run on idle and fast systems. This means the tests will fail when ran on busy systems, or particularly slow systems (be it a raspberrypi1, or a slow qemu). In general I suggest having a way to skip tests that depend on a fast/idle system.

2) Tests sensitive to load because the test has timeouts that are low for no good reason, eg using 100ms when the task being waited for could take 120ms. In this case there's no reason not to bump the timeout to something higher (like 10s) to cater for slow/busy systems.

3) Tests with race conditions that mostly are not noticable. These should be fixed.

I've not yet dug into what categories the tests we're having to skip are, but I wanted to file this ticket to raise it with the strace maintainers to see if you have any thoughts.

title: pwritev/pwrite64 tests fail on musl systems
body:
Following tests fail on musl systems

preadv-pwritev.gen.test'
pread64-pwrite64.gen.test
pwritev.gen.test

The reason being, [musl wraps]( https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/src?id=5370070fded61b569196764673a4fc8440aac79e) pwritev/pwrite64 around `pwritev2`
which means that diffs between exp and out files do not match, since strace tests are
expecting pwritev/pwrite64 syscalls directly.

Perhaps these tests should call the syscalls directly instead of going through libc functions.

Part of this problem is fixed with #347

title: tests: use .code16 to express kvm input directly in real-mode
body: * tests/ioctl_kvm_run_common.c (top-level): Use .code16 int the inline assembly code. Rewrite the code in real-mode notation.

title: tests: make uio test regex work with musl
body:
musl-libc handles the `pwrite` calls differently than glibc, making the uio tests fail. Using glibc, there are separated `pwrite` and `pwritev` calls, however musl uses only `pwritev2` for both `pwrite` and `pwritev`.

To account to this difference, change the verifying regex in way to match both glibc and musl outputs.

Closes #346

title: uio test fails with musl-libc
body:
When running the test suite on a system with musl-libc, the uio test fails:

```
Failed patterns of expected output:
#3: pwrite(64)?\(0, "\\0\\0\\0\\0", 4, 1004211379570065135\) += 4
#4: pwritev\(0, \[\{iov_base="\\0\\0\\0\\0", iov_len=4\}\], 1, 1004211379570065135\) += 4

Actual output:
mmap(0x56381027a000, 4096, PROT_NONE, MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_FIXED|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0) = 0x56381027a000
close(0)                                = 0
open("/dev/zero", O_RDONLY|O_LARGEFILE) = 0
pread64(0, "\0\0\0\0", 4, 1004211379570065135) = 4
preadv(0, [{iov_base="\0\0\0\0", iov_len=4}], 1, 1004211379570065135) = 4
close(0)                                = 0
open("/dev/null", O_WRONLY|O_LARGEFILE) = 0
pwritev2(0, [{iov_base="\0\0\0\0", iov_len=4}], 1, 1004211379570065135, RWF_NOAPPEND) = 4
pwritev2(0, [{iov_base="\0\0\0\0", iov_len=4}], 1, 1004211379570065135, RWF_NOAPPEND) = 4
close(0)                                = 0
+++ exited with 0 +++
uio.test: failed test: ../../src/strace -e%desc ../uio output mismatch
FAIL uio.test (exit status: 1)
```

The reason seems to be the way musl handles the pwrite calls: both `pwrite` and `pwritev` are actually `pwritev2`:
calling `pwrite` calls `pwritev2`: https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/unistd/pwrite.c#n10
calling `pwritev` calls `pwritev2`: https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/unistd/pwritev.c#n10

title: Implement socket decoding using pidfd_getfd (was: propagate unix socket name from bind())
body:
This is for the `--decode-fds=all` option. Currently after a unix socket gets bind()ed a name:
```
bind(103<UNIX:[1629885]>, {sa_family=0x1 /* AF_UNIX */, sun_path=@"my-neat-socket\x00\x00\x00"}, 110 <unfinished ...>
```
that name is not shown in other syscalls involving that fd:
```
listen(103<UNIX:[1629885]>, 4 <unfinished ...>
```
This would be useful because when analyzing a binary you may want to search for all syscalls involving operations on a given socket, and the name of the socket stays consistent between program runs (or if the socket is destroyed/recreated).

title: Decoding of NVIDIA driver ioctls
body:
Hi! I'm interested in adding support for decoding the ioctls used against `/dev/nvidia*`, and I figured I'd open an issue here before I write too much code and see if anyone else is interested in this.

On the userspace side, the ioctls are called by non-free libraries like CUDA (`libcuda.so`) and NVML (`libnvidia-ml.so`, the NVIDIA Management Library), and NVIDIA's GLX library. In turn, they are used by higher-level GPU users like Torch, `nvidia-smi`, and Xorg.

On the kernel side, the ioctls are implemented by both the more common non-free NVIDIA drivers and by the official open-source drivers at https://github.com/NVIDIA/open-gpu-kernel-modules. This repository has a handful of header files defining the interface as well as actual implementation for reference. My understanding is that the code is derived from a common core also used for the non-free drivers and other NVIDIA products.

Google's "gvisor" hypervisor also implements these ioctls for the purpose of securely virtualizing access to the GPU, and in the process they track differences in the ABI across driver versions. They currently handle ABIs from driver versions 535 to 575, and if you look in history they previously handled driver version 525. (I have not looked closely to see what the ABI differences are. Also, this implementation seems to be targeted at the open source driver, although my vague sense is that compatibility is based on the driver version number reported by `__NV_IOWR(NV_ESC_CHECK_VERSION_STR)`, which I think is the same string.) https://github.com/google/gvisor/tree/master/pkg/sentry/devices/nvproxy

Note that these are not the same as the `/dev/nvhost*` interface for which a patch was previously submitted at https://lists.strace.io/pipermail/strace-devel/2020-February/009344.html, which use ioctl type codes `'A`, `G`, `H` (overlaps with hiddev), `N`, and `T` (overlaps with term and soundcard). That seems to be the interface for the Tegra embedded/SOC GPUs. At the moment I'm most interested in (and have access to) the server-class GPUs (formerly "Tesla"), using ioctl type code `F` (no overlap).

I started hacking on this over at geofft/strace branch nvidia, which gets me at least ioctl names:
```
$ strace -P /dev/nvidiactl nvidia-smi 2>&1 >/dev/null | head
stat("/dev/nvidiactl", {st_mode=S_IFCHR|0666, st_rdev=makedev(0xc3, 0xff), ...}) = 0
stat("/dev/nvidiactl", {st_mode=S_IFCHR|0666, st_rdev=makedev(0xc3, 0xff), ...}) = 0
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/dev/nvidiactl", O_RDWR) = 9
fcntl(9, F_SETFD, FD_CLOEXEC)           = 0
ioctl(9, _IOC(_IOC_READ|_IOC_WRITE, 0x46, 0xd2, 0x48), 0x7fffd85b31a0) = 0
ioctl(9, _IOC(_IOC_READ|_IOC_WRITE, 0x46, 0xd6, 0x8), 0x7fffd85b32b0) = 0
ioctl(9, _IOC(_IOC_READ|_IOC_WRITE, 0x46, 0xc8, 0x900), 0x79e3046cc0a0) = 0
ioctl(9, _IOC(_IOC_READ|_IOC_WRITE, 0x46, 0x2b, 0x20), 0x7fffd85b3490) = 0
ioctl(9, _IOC(_IOC_READ|_IOC_WRITE, 0x46, 0x2a, 0x20), 0x7fffd85b29f0) = 0
ioctl(9, _IOC(_IOC_READ|_IOC_WRITE, 0x46, 0x2a, 0x20), 0x7fffd85b29f0) = 0
$ src/strace -P /dev/nvidiactl nvidia-smi 2>&1 >/dev/null | head
stat("/dev/nvidiactl", {st_mode=S_IFCHR|0666, st_rdev=makedev(0xc3, 0xff), ...}) = 0
stat("/dev/nvidiactl", {st_mode=S_IFCHR|0666, st_rdev=makedev(0xc3, 0xff), ...}) = 0
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/dev/nvidiactl", O_RDWR) = 9
fcntl(9, F_SETFD, FD_CLOEXEC)           = 0
ioctl(9, __NV_IOWR(NV_ESC_CHECK_VERSION_STR), 0x7ffe3a970150) = 0
ioctl(9, __NV_IOWR(NV_ESC_SYS_PARAMS), 0x7ffe3a970260) = 0
ioctl(9, __NV_IOWR(NV_ESC_CARD_INFO), 0x7b7166acc0a0) = 0

ioctl(9, __NV_IOWR(NV_ESC_RM_CONTROL), 0x7ffe3a96f9a0) = 0
```

I think my first question is how to handle the header files. They are MIT-licensed, so they _can_ be vendored into the repo if we want. I think I only see one example of consuming headers from outside the mainline kernel, for ZFS, is that correct? That one seems to look at the headers and generate `src/ioctls_zfs.h` which is checked in, but also that only handles ioctl naming (as above) and not the actual parameters. I'm likely to want the header files to decode the parameters into structs too. Is it preferable to vendor them and treat them more like mainline uapi is treated?

title: Add an option for printing syscall parameter names
body:
This is a partial implementation of #155. Using `-N` (mnemonic for "names") or `--arg-names` makes **strace** print the syscall parameter names. These names are taken from the corresponding libc function wrapper man pages. For example, `execve(2)` is declared as:

```c
int execve(const char *pathname, char *const _Nullable argv[], char *const _Nullable envp[]);
```

Given that, the output becomes:

```console
$ strace --arg-names -e trace=execve true
execve(pathname="/usr/bin/true", argv=["true"], envp=0x7ffc1fb49df8 /* 70 vars */) = 0
+++ exited with 0 +++

title: WIP: secontext: fixed retrieval of symlink context and /proc/self/ handling
body:
There were multiple issues with symlink handling.

1. When the path being queried is a symlink, we expect the context of the symlink to be displayed, not the one of the target. Due to this, lgetfilecon() has to be used instead of getfilecon() in selinux_getfilecon().  For selinux_getfdcon(), this doesn't apply because we cannot query a symlink.

2. When in 'mismatch' mode, querying the expected context for symlinks becomes harder, because realpath() cannot be used, since it would resolve the symlink, hence the query would end up on the target instead of the symlink itself. To solve this, only the dirname of the path is resolved.

3. SELinux context queries are performed through prefixing by /proc/<PID>/{root,cwd,fd/<FD>}/. This led to querying strace's namespace instead of PID's namespace when resolving paths such as /proc/self/something, because /proc/self always points to ourselves (hence strace). Because of this /proc/self must be substituted as /proc/<PID> first, but this may not always work, because there could be a "fake" /proc/self" in the path. To solve this, the context query is performed on the substituted path and if there is no result, the original path is queried as fallback.

4. Unrelated to symlinks, there was no distinction between not being able to retrieve the expected context due to some error and not having any known expected context. To solve this, on error, a "??" static context is returned.

title: tests: Reduce expected precision for relative-timestamps tests
body:
Currently we have a very small amount of tolerance around the expected 1.0s sleep time, specifically 0.1s in either direction.

If the machine is not very fast (e.g. StarFive VisionFive 2, a very popular and reasonably performant riscv64 board that's now a couple of years old) and is heavily loaded (e.g. because other builds are running at the same time or the test suite has been executed with 'make -j check'), then the test might fail because of an additional delay that's as small as 0.1s.

Since the test is really intended to ensure that the timestamps are displayed using the requested precision, reporting a failure in this case is not very useful. Instead, we should tolerate delays of up to 1.0s as long as the timestamps are printed out using the expected format.

title: RFE: support different clock sources for timestamps
body:
It is sometimes useful to relate strace to other data sources (e.g. `perf record`), which requires the same clock source to be use on both sides. However strace only support wall clock time for its timestamps.

Maybe an option can be added for choosing the clock source.

title: Include "clock time" in strace call count report
body:
Currently output for "call count report" include: %time, seconds, usec/call, calls, error per syscall. Suggestion adding additional aggregate - "**Time Spent in each call (seconds) **". Either as extra column in the current `-c` report, or as option to extend the current report.

The "Time Spent" in each call is already available as an `-T` option to the 'detailed' report. it provides important value - it shows the cost of the system calls in terms of "Wall time", and not just in terms of kernel CPU time. The most obvious example will be IO calls (read, write, select, open, ...). When analyzing performance of programs - knowing the actual time to complete IO is extremely useful information.

From my experience - only the cumulative value (in seconds) is relevant). No need to average, or % of total.

My current workaround is to running strace in the 'detailed' mode with `-T` - collecting the time from the <NNN> tokens at the end of each line (from the -T), and aggregating it by system call. See example blow: e.g. <0.000068> in the `read` system call. However this approach is inefficient - standard error of strace need to captured into a (large) file, and post-processed. It add lot of overhead to the measuring (compared with the light cost of the -c report).

```
read(0, "4\t./.cache\n24\t./proj/x\n28\t./proj"..., 16384) = 4124 <0.000068>
read(0, "40260\t./proj/ln-pairs/y\n80520\t./"..., 16384) = 46 <0.002553>
read(0, "130896\t./proj\n2704\t./bin\n133708\t"..., 16384) = 34 <0.000069>
read(0, "", 16384)                      = 0 <0.000061>
newfstatat(1, "", {st_mode=S_IFCHR|0620, st_rdev=makedev(0x88, 0), ...}, AT_EMPTY_PATH) = 0 <0.000059>
write(1, "    120     240    4204\n", 24    120     240    4204
) = 24 <0.000085>
close(0)                                = 0 <0.000086>
close(1)                                = 0 <0.000073>
close(2)                                = 0 <0.000071>
exit_group(0)                           = ?
```

title: RFE: provide an alias to the strace command that enables the most useful decoding capabilities
body: strace has gotten quite a few options that enrich its output over the years, but most people know little about those, as they are not enabled by default. One major reason for that is hesitance to change the default output format for strace.  One way it can be addressed is to provide an alias to the strace command, so it gets all the improved decoding capabilities in the interactive sessions, while not affecting strace's usage in scripts.

title: incorerect system call name in "restart_syscall(<... resuming interrupted"
body:

#include <poll.h>

main(void)
{

title: sched_attr: Use Linux types in struct sched_attr
body: The recent addition of struct sched_attr to glibc deliberately used Linux types to simplify porting from `<linux/sched.h>` to `<sched.h>`. Switch the bundled definition here to `__u32` and `__u64` as well.

title: riscv64: First syscall argument missing when GET_SYSCALL_INFO is disabled
body:
Distro packages for strace seem to disable the test suite on riscv64 (see for example [Fedora](http://fedora.riscv.rocks:3000/rpms/strace/src/commit/37fbe25da5896569c05efd0f2b8c4f01010bbe87/strace.spec#L109-L113) and [Debian](https://salsa.debian.org/debian/strace/-/blob/b225a340e2af5fe0cbe035cebb08738eb6b88da8/debian/rules#L59-63)).

I recently tried building the latest Fedora package on riscv64 with test suite enabled and it mostly worked fine, with the exception of a single failure for `tests/legacy_syscall_info.test`. Minimal reproducer that displays the issue:

```
$ ./src/strace /
execve("/", ["/"], 0x3fd7194e00 /* 35 vars */) = -1 EACCES (Permission denied)
./src/strace: exec: Permission denied
+++ exited with 1 +++

$ ./src/disable_ptrace_get_syscall_info ./src/strace /
execve(0xffffffffffffffda, ["/"], 0x3fe6949df0 /* 35 vars */) = -1 EACCES (Permission denied)
./src/strace: exec: Permission denied
+++ exited with 1 +++
```

No matter what program is run under strace and which syscalls it uses, the first argument to any syscall is always reported as `0xffffffffffffffda` when `PTRACE_GET_SYSCALL_INFO` is not available. All the other argument are fine.

I've sprinkled `tprintf_string()` all over the place, notably in `ptrace_setregset()`, and based on what I've seen it's not some code in strace itself that causes the bogus value to be reported: if I inspect `riscv_regs.a0` immediately after calling `strace()`, I can see that the previous value has been overwritten by the syscall.

So either there's a bug in the kernel, or strace needs to do something different to get the actual value of `a0`. Looking at the kernel source I can see that an [`orig_a0`](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/196145c606d0f816fd3926483cb1ff87e09c2c0b/arch/riscv/include/asm/ptrace.h#L52-L53) field exists in `struct pt_regs`, but AFAICT that's private data that we can't get access to from userspace...

I'm afraid this is as far as I'm able to go. Please let me know if I can provide additional information, test tentative patches, or do anything else to help get this fixed.

title: Incorrect  netlink header decode for RTM_GETNEIGH message
body:
When decoding an `RTM_GETNEIGH` message, **strace** interprets the data immediately after the netlink message header as a `struct ifinfomsg`.  However, it is actually a `struct ndmsg`.

See `RTM_GETNEIGH` in https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/rtnetlink.7.html.

Run `strace bridge fdb show br $BRIDGE` to see this behavior.

title: print_utils.h: initialize `hex_chars` as an array, not via string
body:
`gcc-15` added a new warning in https://gcc.gnu.org/PR115185:

    print_utils.h:16:35: error: initializer-string for array of 'char' is too long [-Werror=unterminated-string-initialization]
       16 | static const char hex_chars[16] = "0123456789abcdef";
          |                                   ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

`strace` does not need to store '\0'. We could either initialize the arrays with individual bytes or allocate extra byte for null.

This change initializes the array bytewise.

title: strace: add support for -u UID:GID that bypasses lookup
body:
When building strace statically linked using the "--username" argument will lead to strange errors. The reason is that the calls to getpwnam() and initgroups() will fail because glibc will still try to dlopen() the libnss modules which then fails in unexpected ways.

The `--username` argument is only needed for uid:gid and supplementary groups setup. So this commit provides a way to pass uid:gid via the commandline and it will not init supplementary groups (but it could be extended for this).

This does allow to use a statically linked strace.

title: (Linux) weird double print behaviour on TCGETS/TCSETS ioctl
Fix strace -r during the second after booting
body:
strace -r decides whether the previous timespec has been initialized by
checking if `tv_sec == 0`. However, in the second after booting,
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC` will legitimately have a `tv_sec` of 0. This causes every
displayed timestamp to display as `0.000000` during the second after boot.

Check `tv_nsec` as well before assuming the previous timespec is uninitialized.

-----

Originally discovered in a freshly booted virtual system, amusingly while
trying to use strace to debug a similar issue in ping:
https://github.com/iputils/iputils/pull/499

But there's a little problem: If a syscall is made by a child process, strace prints `[pid  {pid}<{name}>] {rest of line}`, but if the syscall is made by the process started by strace, this part if missing, what makes this more complex to parse. title: Enable `--seccomp-bpf` by default
body:
As mentioned in https://github.com/sunlin7/compile-db-gen/issues/2, adding `--seccomp-bpf` can result in a huge performance improvement. Why not enable it by default?

I understand, that there may be corner cases, when `--seccomp-bpf` has undesirable effects. But the majority of use cases can really benefit from it. For applications/scripts making use of strace and aiming to be compatible across different strace versions it may be too difficult to figure out if `--seccomp-bpf` is supported. It would be very nice to make this decision on strace side.

title: accept vs accept4 syscalls on 32 bit x86
body:
Within Yocto Project we recently set 5.15 as our minimum kernel version. This changes the way glibc is built such that the accept() call changes to use the accept4 syscall behind the scenes. This causes various test failures in accept, net-yy-inet6, net-yy-inet and
net-y-unix. I'm not sure how this should be handled in strace?

As an example:

cat  net-yy-inet6.gen.log
--- exp
+++ out
@@ -5,7 +5,7 @@
 getsockopt(3<TCPv6:[[::1]:46887]>, SOL_TCP, TCP_MAXSEG, [536], [4]) = 0
 socket(AF_INET6, SOCK_STREAM, IPPROTO_IP) = 4<TCPv6:[17255]>
 connect(4<TCPv6:[17255]>, {sa_family=AF_INET6, sin6_port=htons(46887), sin6_flowinfo=htonl(0), inet_pton(AF_INET6, "::1", &sin6_addr), sin6_scope_id=0}, 28) = 0
-accept(3<TCPv6:[[::1]:46887]>, {sa_family=AF_INET6, sin6_port=htons(60152), sin6_flowinfo=htonl(0), inet_pton(AF_INET6, "::1", &sin6_addr), sin6_scope_id=0}, [28]) = 5<TCPv6:[[::1]:46887->[::1]:60152]>
+accept4(3<TCPv6:[[::1]:46887]>, {sa_family=AF_INET6, sin6_port=htons(60152), sin6_flowinfo=htonl(0), inet_pton(AF_INET6, "::1", &sin6_addr), sin6_scope_id=0}, [28], 0) = 5<TCPv6:[[::1]:46887->[::1]:60152]>
 getpeername(5<TCPv6:[[::1]:46887->[::1]:60152]>, {sa_family=AF_INET6, sin6_port=htons(60152), sin6_flowinfo=htonl(0), inet_pton(AF_INET6, "::1", &sin6_addr), sin6_scope_id=0}, [28]) = 0
 getpeername(4<TCPv6:[[::1]:60152->[::1]:46887]>, {sa_family=AF_INET6, sin6_port=htons(46887), sin6_flowinfo=htonl(0), inet_pton(AF_INET6, "::1", &sin6_addr), sin6_scope_id=0}, [28]) = 0
 setsockopt(4<TCPv6:[[::1]:60152->[::1]:46887]>, SOL_TCP, TCP_MAXSEG, [536], 4) = 0
net-yy-inet6.gen.test: failed test: ../../src/strace -a22 -yy -eclose,network ../net-yy-inet6 output mismatch
FAIL net-yy-inet6.gen.test (exit status: 1)

title: strace causes this python3 setup.py install to hang
body:
The Numpy setup install invokes a fairly complex set of child processes when compiling from source.  The install never completes when run within strace.

The process tree at the time of the hang looks like this:
```
   372796 pts/5    S      0:00 strace -f -q -s 1024 -e trace=execve python setup.py install
   372799 pts/5    Z      0:00  \_ [python] <defunct>
   372850 pts/5    D      0:00 /usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/11/collect2 -plugin /usr/lib/gcc/x86_64...
   372851 pts/5    t      0:00  \_ /usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/11/collect2 -plugin /usr/lib/gcc/x8...
```
The kernel stacks for the two gcc processes are
(1) for the parent:
```
# cat /proc/372850/stack
[<0>] kernel_clone+0x1fa/0x3d0
[<0>] __do_sys_vfork+0x40/0x60
[<0>] do_syscall_64+0x5c/0xc0
[<0>] entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x61/0xcb
```
and (2) for the hung child:
```
# cat /proc/372851/stack
[<0>] ptrace_stop+0x189/0x360
[<0>] ptrace_do_notify+0x86/0xb0
[<0>] ptrace_notify+0x55/0x80

[<0>] do_syscall_64+0x37/0xc0

```

title: Test suite breaks on 32 bit platforms when strace is built with '-D_TIME_BITS=64 -D_FILE_OFFSET_BITS=64'
body:
To make 32 bit glibc based platforms prepared for year 2038, all software must be rebuilt with the above flags, which ensure that glibc defines time-sensitive data types with enough bits to go beyond that date.

Unfortunately, this breaks strace's test suite, which would use these data types but continue to directly issue 32 bit versions of system calls. For example, ppoll (first lines are printed by strace, second lines by tests/ppoll - they should match but they aren't):

title: 41GB files in tests output cause troubles for some tools
body:
Hi,

After running "make check" in strace 6.1 and in strace git, the following:

    find -type f -size +1G -exec du -hs {} +

yields:

    0	./tests/clock.dir/stat.sample
    0	./tests/fstat.dir/stat.sample
    0	./tests/fstat-Xabbrev.dir/stat.sample
    0	./tests/fstat-Xraw.dir/stat.sample
    0	./tests/fstat-Xverbose.dir/stat.sample
    [...]

These very large files (66 files are 41GB and 2 files are 1.6GB) are an issue for tools that don't deal with sparse files efficiently, e.g. gnu tar by default (as used by autopkgtest for Debian/Ubuntu). For Ubuntu, I've updated the packaging to truncate files larger than 50MB down to 1MB (iirc) after tests are run (test artifacts are saved).

I've tried to understand what was going on but couldn't spot anything obvious and couldn't dive deep into the tests logic. I think this didn't happen with strace 5.19.

Of course, just as I'm creating this bug report, I'm now seeing that the code responsible for creating these files seems to be in "create_sample(const char *fname, const libc_off_t size)" in tests/xstatx.c and the size is governed by the SAMPLE_SIZE define.

It's possible nothing has changed in strace and it can be either something strace uses or something in the build/test infrastructure of Ubuntu or in Ubuntu in general. Nevertheless, a change in strace is the most likely at this point. Do you know if something related to that could have changed recently in strace? Why use 41GB? Is it because it's obviously over 4GB? Any idea or pointer?

Thanks.

title: strauss: add missing line separators
mips: fix raw_syscall_0
body:
Some of the tests use a custom function (raw_syscall_0) for syscall invocation.

The implementation for mips was flawed: it unconditionally clobbered "hi" and "lo", which is not valid for MIPS R6, because these targets lack those registers w/o DSP extension.

GCC 10+ refuses to compile such constructs: [1], [2].

Fix the syscall invocation implementation for mips.

[1] https://gcc.gnu.org/git/?p=gcc.git&a=commit;h=0a59215131c02dee4c8829f93d1ee678647614da
[2] https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=91233

* src/linux/mips/raw_syscall.h: Add SYSCALL_CLOBBERLIST.
(raw_syscall_0): Use it.

title: Add a configure flag for installing tests
body:
--enable-install-test-binaries=yes installs binaries from the test suite to $libexec/strace.

This flag does not install everything necessary to run the tests (no harness), but at least installs the binaries.

This can be useful when debugging various targets
and how strace behaves on them.

This can also be extended later with a standalone test harness that would not depend on the build directory to be present on the target.

* configure.ac: Add --enable-install-test-binaries.
* tests/Makefile.am: Add testslibexecdir, testslibexec_PROGRAMS.

title: madvise constant differences on parisc removed in Linux 6.2
arch_prctl: non-mainline ARCH_CET_* constants are not recognized
body:
Thanks for this semi-magical tool!

Strace doesn't support value `0x3001` as the subfunction to `arch_prctl` system call, and prints `"ARCH_???"` instead. It looks like it is a new glibc feature that utilizes shadow stack: https://codebrowser.dev/glibc/glibc/sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/x86/include/asm/prctl.h.html

Any chance it is going to be added in the near future?

body:
This is the successor patch-set sent in the last year (https://lists.strace.io/pipermail/strace-devel/2022-March/011014.html)

Though I got a review on the mailing list, revising the patch set was too hard for me at that time.

----

```
IOCTL command assignments are overwrapped.
We can observe the overwrapping when running vi under strace:

  ioctl(0, SNDCTL_TMR_START or TCSETS, {B38400 opost -isig -icanon -echo ...}) = 0
----------------------------^^

We can remove the ambiguity if strace knows about the object behind a
given file descriptor. In the above example, whether the fd (0) is
associated with a sound device or a terminal is the hint for removing
the ambiguity.

We don't have to develop new code for getting the hint from scratch;
the code implementing -y option gathers information about fd already.

  ioctl(0</dev/pts/26<char 136:26>>, TCSETS, {B38400 opost -isig -icanon -echo ...}) = 0
----------------------^^^^^^^^^^^

Currently, the information gathered with -y option is used only for
printing.  This patch-set utilizes the information for improving the
quality of decoding.

With the patch-set, strace reports the ioctl as following:

  ioctl(0, TCSETS, {B38400 opost -isig -icanon -echo ...}) = 0
```

title: Add some kfd ioctl decoding

kfd (/dev/kfd) is an interface exposed by amdgpu kernel driver for user space drivers (e.g. ROCm)

KD and KFD both use the 'K' base. Fortunately they currently do not overlap and can be distinguished from NR. However, as KFD is gradually adding ioctls, one day they may overlap.

More generously, how do we decode ioctls arg with the same base? We already have `ioctl_next_match` for displaying ioctls with the same code, do we have similar mechanisms?

### Note

TODOs in code will not be addressed in this patchset. They could be implemented later when I get the time.

Also, the variable length array handling for `struct kfd_ioctl_svm_attribute attrs[];` could be generalized to e.g. `defs.h` then `print_field.h`. I think `tfetch_obj` after the end of the struct is quite unsafe. If kernel returned an invalid `nattr`, e.g. -1, then we will access the whole memory. What's your opinion on this.

title: Add structured output
body:
Add options "-B / --structured-output FORMAT" to print the output of strace in a more parsable format. Currently, we provide "json" for JSON format and "ocaml" for OCaml format.

Given the extend of modifications, we don't aim at covering all the features of strace, but only the most commonly used, and keep full textual backward compatibility.

JSON Format definition:

The format can be checked by putting it in a contest "[... null]", as an array of syscalls. All ints are stored in strings to avoid overflows and specific notations.

OCaml Format definition:

```
terminals:= token_string | token_integerL

struct := "[" [ token_string "," value ';' ]* "]"
array := "[" [ value ";" ]* "]"
value :=
| "NULL"
| "STRING" token_string
| "PARTIAL_STRING" token_string
| "ARRAY" array
| "INDIRECT" array
| "INT" token_integer
| "STRUCT" struct
| "FLAGS" array
| "CALL" "(" token_string "," array ")"
```

Values can be typechecked by the OCaml compiler using the following ADT: 

```
type t =
  | NULL
  | PARTIAL_STRING of string
  | STRING of string
  | INT of int64
  | INDIRECT of t list
  | ARRAY of t list
  | FLAGS of t list
  | STRUCT of ( string * t ) list
  | CALL of string * t list
  | ARG of string * t
```

Makefile uses `sed -r` which isn't POSIX standard.
body:
The [src/Makefile.am](https://github.com/strace/strace/blob/a0f7df7d3783074b5aac66ea4e55646524164e70/src/Makefile.am) and some build shell scripts use `sed -r` which isn't POSIX standard.  Newer versions of GNU sed recommend using `-E` instead: https://www.gnu.org/software/sed/manual/sed.html#Command_002dLine-Options

> Historically this was a GNU extension, but the -E extension has since been added to the POSIX standard (http://austingroupbugs.net/view.php?id=528), so use -E for portability. GNU sed has accepted -E as an undocumented option for years, and *BSD seds have accepted -E for years as well, but scripts that use -E might not port to other older systems.

`sed -r` also appears in a number test-related scripts, but their appearance there don't interfere with the build process.

title: printsiginfo: decode si_pkey field
body:
This adds decoding of `si_pkey` field  which is set on `SIGSEGV` in case
of memory access violation on some modern CPUs (these have `pku` flag in `/proc/cpuinfo`).

Here's few sample outputs:

```
pkey_alloc(0, 0)                        = 3
pkey_mprotect(0x7f3f20662000, 4096, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, 3) = 0
--- SIGSEGV {si_signo=SIGSEGV, si_code=SEGV_PKUERR, si_addr=0x7f3f20662000, si_pkey=3} ---
```
or another case:
```
mmap(NULL, 4096, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0) = 0x7f137374b000
mprotect(0x7f137374b000, 4096, PROT_EXEC) = 0
--- SIGSEGV {si_signo=SIGSEGV, si_code=SEGV_PKUERR, si_addr=0x7f137374b000, si_pkey=1} ---
```

title: Implement displaying of expected context upon mismatch
body:
New option to `--secontext=...`
- `mismatch`: print expected context on mismatch

When using `mismatch`, an additional check is made on the context by reading the context database and comparing the output after stripping the unwanted part (e.g. stripping nothing in `full` mode, keeping the type only in default / `short` mode):
- if it differs, prints the expected context after print '!!'
- if not, don't print anything

Example with `/home/rmetrich/GIT/strace/autom4te.cache/output.3` file:

~~~
$ matchpathcon /home/rmetrich/GIT/strace/autom4te.cache/output.3
/home/rmetrich/GIT/strace/autom4te.cache/output.3	unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0

$ ls -Z /home/rmetrich/GIT/strace/autom4te.cache/output.3
system_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0 /home/rmetrich/GIT/strace/autom4te.cache/output.3
~~~

From above, we see the user part differs (`unconfined_u` vs `system_u`)

Output in `!full` mode (no mismatch found since diff is only on the type):

~~~
$ strace --secontext=mismatch -e statx stat /home/rmetrich/GIT/strace/autom4te.cache/output.3
... statx(AT_FDCWD, "/home/rmetrich/GIT/strace/autom4te.cache/output.3" [user_home_t], ...
~~~

Output in `full` mode (diff found on user):

~~~
... statx(AT_FDCWD, "/home/rmetrich/GIT/strace/autom4te.cache/output.3" [system_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0!!unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0], ...
~~~

title: Print cwd path to AT_FDCWD when -y (--decode-fd=path) flag is used
body:
When syscalls use *AT_FDCWD* (e.g. `openat()`), it's not always obvious to determine the current directory, one need to search back for any `chdir()` syscall, in the process or some parent.

This patch prints the path when `-y` (`--decode-fd=path`) flag is used, e.g.:
~~~
openat(AT_FDCWD</home/rmetrich/GIT/strace>, "/lib64/libselinux.so.1" ...)
~~~

Note the initial commit only printed when `-y` was specified, but it appears that apparently the path decoding for FDs is always performed, even when `--decode-fd=dev` only is specified for example, hence the final code proposes to keep this behaviour:
as soon as `--decode-fd` is used, *AT_FDCWD* gets decoded.

This explains the 2 source code commits, all this can be merged if necessary later.

title: Introduce -Y option for printing command names for PIDs
body:
In some applications like qemu-kvm, threads change their
command names to indicate their roles in the application.
Users can access the command name via /proc/$pid/comm.
The command name can be a great hit to understand the application
behavior.
    
This pull request introduces -Y option that enables printing command
names where PIDs appear.
    
For example (without -Y option):

```
# src/strace -e poll,ioctl -f -p "$(pidof qemu-system-x86_64)"
[pid 254329] ioctl(18, KVM_RUN <unfinished ...>
[pid 254332] ioctl(21, KVM_RUN <unfinished ...>
[pid 254331] ioctl(20, KVM_RUN <unfinished ...>
[pid 254330] ioctl(19, KVM_RUN <unfinished ...>
[pid 254309] poll([{fd=9, events=POLLOUT}], 1, 0) = 1 ...
[pid 254309] poll([{fd=9, events=POLLOUT}], 1, 0) = 1 ...
```

(with -Y option):

```
# src/strace -e poll,ioctl -Y -f -p "$(pidof qemu-system-x86_64)"
[pid 254329<CPU 0/KVM>] ioctl(18, KVM_RUN <unfinished ...>
[pid 254332<CPU 3/KVM>] ioctl(21, KVM_RUN <unfinished ...>
[pid 254331<CPU 2/KVM>] ioctl(20, KVM_RUN <unfinished ...>
[pid 254330<CPU 1/KVM>] ioctl(19, KVM_RUN <unfinished ...>
[pid 254309<qemu-system-x86>] poll([{fd=9, events=POLLOUT}], 1, 0) = 1 ...
[pid 254309<qemu-system-x86>] poll([{fd=9, events=POLLOUT}], 1, 0) = 1 ...
```

This change considers only PIDs in the prefixes of trace lines.
Printing command names for PIDs in arguments and return values is
future work.

title: Bundled linux/prctl.h missing the PR_SET_VMA macro needed for Android
body:
Bundled `linux/prctl.h` in version 5.13 is missing the `PR_SET_VMA` macro needed for Android, and thus building strace for Android is broken.
```
aarch64-linux-android21-clang -DHAVE_CONFIG_H   -I./linux/aarch64 -I./linux/aarch64 -I./linux/generic -I./linux/generic -I. -I. -I../bundled/linux/arch/arm64/include/uapi -I ../bundled/linux/include/uapi -DIN_STRACE=1      -Isrc/linux/generic  -I./bundled/linux/arch/arm64/include/uapi -I./bundled/linux/include/uapi -Wall -Wextra -Wno-missing-field-initializers -Wno-unused-parameter -Wdate-time -Wformat-security -Winit-self -Winitializer-overrides -Wmissing-prototypes -Wnested-externs -Wold-style-definition -Wundef -Wwrite-strings   -g -O2 -MT libstrace_a-prctl.o -MD -MP -MF .deps/libstrace_a-prctl.Tpo -c -o libstrace_a-prctl.o `test -f 'prctl.c' || echo './'`prctl.c
In file included from prctl.c:18:
./xlat/prctl_options.h:190:7: error: use of undeclared identifier 'PR_SET_VMA'
 XLAT(PR_SET_VMA),
      ^
./xlat/prctl_options.h:201:10: error: invalid application of 'sizeof' to an incomplete type 'const struct xlat_data []'
 .size = ARRAY_SIZE(prctl_options_xdata),
         ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
./macros.h:17:32: note: expanded from macro 'ARRAY_SIZE'
# define ARRAY_SIZE(a_) (sizeof(a_) / sizeof((a_)[0]) + MUST_BE_ARRAY(a_))
                               ^~~~
```

title: configure --enable-mpers=check fails to detect certain local misconfigurations
Rewrite time-sensitive checks to compare test's time notion with strace's
body:
sleep/nanosleep/-r/-t/-T/delay/syscall stats checks rely on the fact that the nanosleep call (or its equivalents) wakes up the process within some tolerance, usually 0.1—0.2 seconds. This is not the case in some virtualised environments with heavy over-provisioning, one notable example is s390, which results in test failures which are not indicative of strace's issues (but rather some intermittent issues with the environment).

One possible fix for this is to collect the experienced delay from the test program's PoV and compare it to strace's notion of the time passed.

Via https://lists.strace.io/pipermail/strace-devel/2021-April/010501.html

title: Strace should prevent a process under tracing to attach to the strace itself
body:
There is a problem when mutual debugging of 2 processes can stuck in unkillable stopped state.

When one process, let's say "A", is tracing the another process "B", and the process "B" is trying to attach to the process "A", then both of them are getting stuck in the "t+" state. And they are ignoring all of the signals including the SIGKILL, so it is not possible to terminate them without a reboot.

To reproduce:
1) Open two terminals.
2) Attach with `strace -p ...` from the first terminal to the shell (bash) of the second terminal.
3) In the second terminal run `exec strace -p ...` to attach to the PID of the first strace.

Then you'll see that the second strace is hanging without any output. And the first strace will output following and hang too:
```
ptrace(PTRACE_SEIZE, 11795, NULL, PTRACE_O_TRACESYSGOOD|PTRACE_O_TRACEEXEC|PTRACE_O_TRACEEXIT
```
(The 11795 is the PID of the first strace itself.)

And in the process list you will see following:
```
ps awux | grep strace
user   11776  0.0  0.0  24752  2248 pts/3    t+   13:53   0:00 strace -p 11795
user   11795  0.0  0.0  24752  3888 pts/1    t+   13:54   0:00 strace -p 11776
```

I've sent a letter to linux-trace-devel mailing list. But the strace itself is able to forbid to attaching to itself, at least when it sees such an attempt.

title: Feature request: Limit the depth of forks following
body:
Currently it is possible only to not attach to child processes at all or to follow forks infinitely. Sometimes something like `strace -f1 ...` could be useful if a process is launched by some other launcher (like systemd), but you are not interested in tracing of all its descendants, except of the main process. So the option that would allow to limit followed process tree depth could be useful.
Real use case: I need to debug how the system session "systemd" is starting the user session "systemd". But I don't want to log of how the user session "systemd" starts all of the user services.

title: Cannot specify more than one -einject=<...>:<...>:when=<...> expression for a single syscall
body:
For example, currently, invoking strace like this:
```
strace -einject=chdir:retval=1000:when=1 \
       -einject=chdir:retval=2000:when=2
```
injects 2000 at the second occurence of `chdir`, but ignores the first inject expression.

Considering overlapping expressions, when invoked for example like this:
```
strace -einject=<...>:<...>:when=first+step1 \
       -einject=<...>:<...>:when=first+step2
```
strace should perform both injections on steps `first+step1*step2`, in the order from first specified to last specified.

title: Add -e inject=<...>:poke_{enter,exit}=<...> functionality
Structured output
body:
_The following post is subject to change; all the changes will be reflected below the post with a timestamp and a short summary._

_Structured_ is an idea of decoupling the decoding process from the process of outputting, with the intention of being able to choose between different output "drivers". The main motivation is that the current output format is far from being machine-readable. See https://github.com/strace/strace/labels/project%2Fstructured.

The goal of this issue is to document and coordinate the efforts of making strace _structured_, for people who aren't that immersed in strace development that still might want to contribute, and also for those who still remember the original _structured_ and want to see how it is doing.

An attempt of making strace _structured_ was made several years ago, but the changeset never got merged, as big changesets often do. I argue that all further work should be done upstream, with every change going through the review process and getting merged before more changes based on the given change are prepared.

I personally see _structured_ being implemented in three distinct steps.

* First, abstract all the printing away with PRINT_* macros, implementing more if a need arises.
  * Even though the process of abstracting printing away is already ongoing, there's still a lot of `tprint*` present in the parsers. There should be none.
* Second, separate the printing part and the parsing part into different compilation units.
  * There is, it seems, a demand for having strace as a library (#70). The output drivers can be seen as different "frontends" in this case. Presenting strace as a library poses a lot of non-_structured_-related challenges, though.
* Third, implement other output drivers, for example, provide a reference machine-readable output driver. The standard driver can also be consistently modified at this point.

Some, even if vague, vision of the future API is useful at the first step, to have less shuffly-replacey work at the second step. For this reason I would love to hear thoughts on this. Maybe the output drivers should be the libraries instead. Maybe "driver" is not the best name for them. Maybe other backends are already on the horizon and should be taken into account too.

title: Should IPPROTO_MAX be updated?
body:
The latest version of musl updated `IPPROTO_MAX` in `/usr/include/netinet/in.h` to '263' after the addition of `IPPROTO_MPTCP`, which has a value of '262'.

Strace also [added IPPROTO_MPTCP](2c721018cc3351ee4518f4f57bbf5b646f96d533), but `IPPROTO_MAX` was not updated. This causes an assert to fail on Alpine Linux:

```
xlat/inet_protocols.h:242:1: error: static assertion failed: "IPPROTO_MAX != 256"
  242 | static_assert((IPPROTO_MAX) == (256), "IPPROTO_MAX != 256");
```

The question is, does it make sense to update `IPPROTO_MAX`, like musl did, or not. If it makes sense, but strace has not updated it due to compatibility with glibc, I can patch the strace definition on Alpine Linux for the time being to match. But if there is a good reason not to update it, musl will probably revert that change.

One hint I found in the [Linux source](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/tools/include/uapi/linux/in.h#L83). There `IPPROTO_MAX` is defined after `IPPROTO_MPTCP` in the enum, indicating the value equals to '263'.

title: <linux/bsg.h> requires / used to require <linux/types.h>
body:
I'm building on an old system, where sg_io_v4.c (and tests/ioctl_sg_io_v4.c) fails with
```
/usr/include/linux/bsg.h:11: error: expected specifier-qualifier-list before ‘__s32’
```
and therefore `struct sg_io_v4` isn't resolved. It turns out that `__s32` is defined in `<linux/types.h>`. If I include that right before `<linux/bsg.h>`, strace builds fine.

I'm not sure whether you would change this in configure.ac (as in 3857665065f09f750bfcdd150930e663291b6616) or in the respective source files (as in commit 7bbf7813f9304d935e1f96b259b834789ad457ef). Therefore no pull request from me. ;)

title: Feature request: Print process info on joining to a PID or spawning a new process
body:
Currently when you are attaching to several processes, it is hard to find later what these processes are, what privileges they have, what open file descriptors they inherited, etc. It could be useful to print some process information summary on joining ne PID and on the forking/cloning. The most interesting information (from my point of view) is:
- UIDs,
- GIDs,
- supplementary groups,
- capabilities (effective and permitted),
- open file descriptors,
- command line and executable name.

So when you start to read a tracing log, it would be easier to understand the starting state.

title: Feature request: Multiline syscalls output with syscall argument names and hexdumping buffer arguments
Feature request: annotate sockets based on its destination
body:
Currently when you use options `-y` to annotate file names and socckets in the syscalls arguments it works good for the regular files (and makes life much easier! :+1:) but it could be improved for UNIX and network sockets. Currently you can see: something like:
```
accept4(3<socket:[15157]>, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(62958), sin_addr=inet_addr("1.2.3.4")}, [16], SOCK_CLOEXEC) = 29<socket:[91704707]>
open("/srv/www/i/moon.jpg", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = 30</srv/www/test.jpg>
...
sendfile(29<socket:[91704707]>, 30</srv/www/test.jpg>, [0], 21952) = 21952
```
So it's not clear from the sendfile line, what is the 29-th file description (or socket's 91704707) destination is? It could be shown like this for better understanding:
`sendfile(29<socket:[91704707,AF_INET,1.2.3.4:62958]>, 30</srv/www/test.jpg>, [0], 21952) = 21952`

title: Feature request: name log files based on the executable name
body:
When you are tracing multiple different processes (with `-f -ff` options) when trying to understand what a system does, it is difficult later to understand what log file belongs to what process. There could be an option for automatic renaming the logs based on `argv[0]` supplied to `execve` syscall. I.e. with the proposed options you would get logs named like:
- bash-1234.log
- cp-1235.log

To make it possible, strace needs to:
1) read executable name at the time of attaching to some PID,
2) on the forking and cloning inherit that name,
3) but rename a file on `execve`.

title: Feature request: Display the full syscall line on resuming
body:
Currently when tracing multiple processes you could see something like:
```
[pid  1905] select(0, NULL, NULL, NULL, {0, 198904} <unfinished ...>
[pid 23966] ftruncate(28, 25165824)     = 0
[pid 32266] epoll_wait(20,  <unfinished ...>
[pid  1905] <... select resumed> )      = 0 (Timeout)
```
So on resuming you often need to scroll back to understand of what syscall was continued. especially when you see that resumed syscall failed with some error. So may be there could be an option, so the output could be something like this:
```
[pid  1905] select(0, NULL, NULL, NULL, {0, 198904} <unfinished ...>
[pid 23966] ftruncate(28, 25165824)     = 0
[pid 32266] epoll_wait(20,  <unfinished ...>
[pid  1905] <resumed> select(0, NULL, NULL, NULL, {0, 198904})      = 0 (Timeout)
```
It would make reading the logs easier.

title: sizeof() vs. strlen() issue when composing path in getfdproto()
body:
This [Stack Overflow question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/63464497/what-is-the-size-of-proc-u-fd-u/63464598?noredirect=1#comment112224687_63464598) lead to an observation by [bruno](https://stackoverflow.com/users/2458991/bruno) that the [following code](https://github.com/strace/strace/blob/master/util.c#L487) is incorrect:

```c
char path[sizeof("/proc/%u/fd/%u") + 2 * sizeof(int)*3];
```

Where `sizeof("...")` obviously returns the same size for everything, that being of a `char*` pointer.

This should be:

```c
char path[strlen("/proc/%u/fd/%u") + 2 * sizeof(int)*3];
```

The difference here is enough you could force a buffer overflow with unexpectedly large values for PID and FD.

Another thing to note is that string is also duplicated, used later in the code, and could be assigned to a variable that's used in both places. There's a potential for a mistake here when one is changed but the other is not.

title: No way to distinguish SYS_socketcall from broken-down socket syscalls
body:
`strace` prints both forms of the socket syscalls - the legacy ones multiplexed on `SYS_socketcall`, and the modern individual syscalls - identically, and does not seem to offer any option to distinguish them. This makes it really difficult to debug issues caused by which version a binary is using, e.g. incompatibility with an older kernel that lacks the new syscalls, or behavior of fallback if the caller supports both.

A nice general solution might be adding an option to print the syscall number for all syscalls. I'm not sure if an option specific to `socketcall` makes sense, but at this point it might make sense to just *always* print the old ones as `socketcall(...` and the new ones with their names. I'm not attached to any particular solution, but I think something should be done to resolve the ambiguity and make it possible to debug these syscalls.

title: Autostop conditions?
body:
I feel it would be useful especially for `strace -p` if `strace` had autostop conditions, similarly to how `tshark` does it:

```
       -a  <capture autostop condition>
           Specify a criterion that specifies when TShark is to stop writing
           to a capture file.  The criterion is of the form test:value, where
           test is one of:

           duration:value Stop writing to a capture file after value seconds
           have elapsed.

           filesize:value Stop writing to a capture file after it reaches a
           size of value kB.  If this option is used together with the -b
           option, TShark will stop writing to the current capture file and
           switch to the next one if filesize is reached.  When reading a
           capture file, TShark will stop reading the file after the number of
           bytes read exceeds this number (the complete packet  will be read,
           so more bytes than this number may be read).  Note that the
           filesize is limited to a maximum value of 2 GiB.

           files:value Stop writing to capture files after value number of
           files were written.
```

Useful would be IMO:

- stop after having captured N events
- stop after having written an `-o` output file of more than N bytes
- stop after having run for N seconds

I'm currently trying to get to the bottom of an issue where a long-running daemon process seems to get stuck in an endless loop after receiving a certain packet from the network, and an autostop condition would stop `strace` from filling up the disk when the endless loop begins.

title: Support interval specification in when-expression.
body:
Currently, strace allows syscall tampering only for syscall with 1) fixed invocation index or 2) all invocations starting from n-th (possibly with some step). 

Such two options do not cover a useful scenario of testing retrying/backoffing policy of traced program, which may be done by introducing delays/errors on first n invocations, and then stopping tampering.

This PR adds possibility to invoke strace like the following:

```
strace -e inject=recvfrom:delay_exit=100000:when=3,100 ./bin
```

which results in invocations from third to hundredth (inclusive) being tampered. Formally, syntax now looks like `when=first[,last][+step]`.

This change does not affect the existing behavior.

title: Need option to hook child process exit routine and print getrusage()
body:
When tracing batch jobs (like `make(1)`) it's immesurably useful to get also user/kernel CPU time for each process/thread beside overall clock time for whole process (which we can obtain as difference between `execve` and `+++ exit code` times.

Note: hooking `wait` in parent process is useless, because it won't help with detached threads and daemonized children. And often used `wait4(..., NULL)` won't pass `rusage` back anyway.

Expectations are to print plain list of values in `struct rusage` order:
```strace
180535 1582654045.919886 +++ exited with 0 +++ [4.232111, 0.0, ...]
```
How hard is it to implement?

title: printrusage is time64-incompatible
body:
The `printrusage` code uses the `<sys/resource.h>` `struct rusage` type to print the structure, but this need not match the kernel ABI type used by the syscall, and will not match on 32-bit archs with 64-bit `time_t`.

In this case using `<linux/resource.h>` would not help; it's also using `struct timeval` rather than something that will match the syscall. I'm not sure what the right fix is aside from hard-coding a struct in strace source.

title: Print SELinux contexts when enabling "--secontext" (not compatible with "-c").
body:
This is very useful when debugging SELinux issues, in particular when a process runs in an unexpected context or didn't transition properly, or typically when a file being opened has not the proper context.

Sub-option `--typeonly` may be used to only print the type, as shown in the examples below:

Without any option (standard strace, here used `-fttTvyy` flags):
~~~
118104  16:52:11.141122 select(9, [4<TCP:[0.0.0.0:22]> 6<TCPv6:[[::]:22]>], NULL, NULL, NULL) = 1 (in [4]) <1.845416>
119820  16:52:13.133319 openat(AT_FDCWD, "/home/rmetrich/.ssh/authorized_keys", O_RDONLY|O_NONBLOCK) = 11</home/rmetrich/.ssh/authorized_keys> <0.000399>
~~~

With `--secontext` option, a new column is added after PID, showing the context the PID is executing and each PATH has its context associated (when file exists) :
~~~
118104 [system_u:system_r:sshd_t:s0-s0:c0.c1023] 16:52:11.141122 select(9, [4<TCP:[0.0.0.0:22]> 6<TCPv6:[[::]:22]>], NULL, NULL, NULL) = 1 (in [4]) <1.845416>
119820 [system_u:system_r:sshd_t:s0-s0:c0.c1023] 16:52:13.133319 openat(AT_FDCWD, "/home/rmetrich/.ssh/authorized_keys" [system_u:object_r:nfs_t:s0], O_RDONLY|O_NONBLOCK) = 11</home/rmetrich/.ssh/authorized_keys> [system_u:object_r:nfs_t:s0] <0.000399>
~~~

With `--typeonly` sub-option, same except only the type is displayed:
~~~
118104 [sshd_t] 16:52:11.141122 select(9, [4<TCP:[0.0.0.0:22]> 6<TCPv6:[[::]:22]>], NULL, NULL, NULL) = 1 (in [4]) <1.845416>
119820 [sshd_t] 16:52:13.133319 openat(AT_FDCWD, "/home/rmetrich/.ssh/authorized_keys" [nfs_t], O_RDONLY|O_NONBLOCK) = 11</home/rmetrich/.ssh/authorized_keys> [nfs_t] <0.000399>
~~~

title: sysvipc handling is time64-incompatible
body:
(Apologies if this is a duplicate of something already reported here or elsewhere. I could have sworn I already reported and had communication about it, but I can't find record of that anywhere.)

strace gets the structure definitions and command macro values from `sys/ipc.h`, `sys/sem.h`, etc. only falling back to the kernel uapi headers if these are missing. However, for moving 32-bit archs to 64-bit `time_t`, the application-facing/libc types for `semid_ds`, etc. must necessarily mismatch the kernel types since the existing time fields lack correct alignment (and on some archs, even lack padding) to be expanded/used in-place.

Since strace wants to be working with the structures and command numbers present in the tracee's interface with the kernel, not its own interface with libc, it should be including the kernel uapi headers for these definitions.

Original report and analysis was on the musl libc list in regards to time64 conversion: https://www.openwall.com/lists/musl/2019/10/29/7
